chunks: Ali from his father from Safwan said: I asked Al-Rida (peace be upon him). And Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Ahmad from Safwan and Ahmad ibn Abi Nasr said: We asked Al-Rida (peace be upon him)

About a man who bequeathed to you a share from his wealth, and we do not know what that share is. He said: 'You do not have anything in what has reached you from Ja'far, nor from Abu Ja'far, regarding it.'
We said to him: May Allah ransom us for you, we did not hear our companions mention anything of this from your fathers (peace be upon them). He said: 'The share is one of eight.'
We said to him: May Allah ransom us for you, how did it become one of the eight? He said: 'Do you not read the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?'
I said: I am ransomed for you, I do read it, but I do not know which place it is.

The saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: 'Zakat expenditures are only for the poor and for the needy and for those employed for it and for bringing hearts together and for freeing captivity and for the debt and in the cause of Allah and for the [stranded] traveler - a duty imposed by Allah.'
Then he made a knot with his hand for eight and said: 'And thus the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) divided it into eight shares, so the share is one of eight.'
ai.seo_question: What does 'a share' mean in an ambiguous bequest according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Sahih al-Tusi, Imam al-Rida clarifies that an ambiguous bequest of 'a share' refers to one of the eight specific categories of zakat recipients, linking the legal ruling directly to the Quranic verse 9:60. The Imam physically enumerates the eight parts to demonstrate that the Prophet Muhammad divided zakat into eight equal shares, establishing a precedent for interpreting vague bequests in Shia jurisprudence. This hadith is significant for resolving ambiguity in wills by anchoring the definition of 'share' in established Quranic taxonomy rather than arbitrary division.
